newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian ad revenues seen slumping next year.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian ad revenues seen slumping next year.

text.p: Bulgaria's economic crisis will reduce advertising revenues next year, advertisers said on Monday.

"When you have a shrinking gross domestic product (GDP) the advertising business also shrinks. Our estimates show advertising spending will go down next year," said Christian Lainer, General Manager of Ogilvy & Mather Sofia office.
Lainer was speaking at an annual meeting of local advertisers organised by the Association of Advertising Agencies (AAA), which groups some 40 major local and international ad companies.
"We expect advertising spending to shrink by some 50 percent next year," said AAA Chairman Krasimir Gergov at the same meeting.
"Only the big international advertisers will be able to operate in the Bulgarian market to service their long-term goals in the region...smaller ones may fall out," said Gergov.
Bulgaria's sharply devalued national currency, the lev, has made many western products unaffordable for the average Bulgarian.
The lev has collapsed from 70 to the dollar in January to around 500 to the dollar on Monday. First half-year GDP has fallen by six percent and is seen falling by a further eight percent next year.
Lev equivalent prices of imported beverages and tobacco products, cosmetics, confectionery and detergents have become incompatible with shrinking wages.

"All imported products have became luxury and only five percent of the population can afford them," said Misha Lukic, managing director of the Sofia partner office of Saatchi & Saatchi, which is owned by Britain's Cordiant Plc.

Saatchi, which handles the advertising accounts of big international clients around the world such as British American Tobacco, Master Foods and Procter & Gamble sees its gross advertising turnover for this year falling to $2.5 million in Bulgaria from around $3.5 million in 1995, said Lukic.
"Proctor and Gamble was active only four months this year and spent less than half of their budget in this country," Lukic told Reuters.

Bulgaria which has the lowest level of foreign investment in the region due to excessive red tape, inconsistently applied legislation and rampant organised crime, also suffers the lowest spending on media advertising.
Last year media spending in Bulgaria totalled $56 million compared to $380 million in the Czech Republic, $382 million in Hungary and $580 million in Poland, said Lainer.
Media spending per capita amounted to $6.7 in Bulgaria compared to $36.3 in the Czech Republic and $57.1 in Poland, said Lainer.

Bulgaria is currently debating the introduction of a tough financial regime, called currency board, proposed by the International Monetary Fund to boost economic recovery by curbing inflation and restoring confidence in the lev.

Investors have welcomed the plan hoping it will restore much needed stability and confidence in the crumbling economy, but analysts warn that unless it is accompanied by radical restructuring, the currency board may fail. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
